en: The Dhyānabindu Upaniṣad.
"May He protect us both"—this is the Peace (Śānti).
The Majesty of the Yoga of Meditation on Brahman.
Even if sin were as vast as a mountain, extending for many yojanas, it is pierced by the yoga of meditation; there is never any other means of piercing it. (1)
The seed-syllable is the supreme bindu, and nāda is situated above it;
when the syllable, along with its sound, has ceased, there is the soundless, supreme state. (2)
But that sound which is unstruck (anāhata), and that which is beyond that sound—he who finds that supreme state is a yogi whose doubts are severed. || 3 ||
Having meditated upon the expansion [of the universe], they have gone to that which is Brahman alone through the realization that nothing remains but themselves;
I contemplate that very state of being as my own self, which is the fruit of knowing the reality of Yoga.
Indeed, this *Dhyānabindu Upaniṣad*, which is a division of the *Kṛṣṇayajurveda*,
culminates in the non-dual Brahman alone; it illuminates the meaning of the internal *praṇava* and reveals its means—
the *ajāpā-haṃsa-vidyā*— as well as its further means, the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅga-yoga*).
It has commenced. A commentary on it is now begun from its very brief text.

Its introduction and other preliminary matters are to be inferred as being similar to those of the *Kaṭhavallī* and other texts. First, the Śruti, having first revealed the general primary fruit of meditation-yoga (*dhyānayoga*), [proceeds].
It reveals the nature of Brahman as devoid of distinctions— [as expressed by the verse beginning] "If":
if there exists in any yogi whatsoever a mountain of sin, accumulated over infinite millions of births, vast, extending for many *yojanas*, and difficult to pierce, even that [he destroys].
By means of the yoga of meditation on the *vajra*, the *ṭaṅka*, and the *upabrahman*, [the body] is split and cut into pieces as small as sesame seeds.

The meaning is that without such a yoga of meditation, there is never any other means of splitting or a splitter. (1) Thus, he describes the nature of the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) for this yoga of meditation: "The seed... and so forth.

The *praṇava* is indeed the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*), consisting of the letters *a*, *u*, *m*, and the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*); yet that which is beyond it transcends the *bindu*, *nāda*, *kalā*, and *kalātīta*. The meaning is this: above that *praṇava*, which is the expansion of sound (*śabdaprapañca*) characterized by such distinctions, there exists that which stands as devoid of distinctions—that is the "soundless" (*niḥśabda*).

The word "sa" (with) refers to sound (*praṇava*). The word "ca" (and) serves to indicate that which is denoted by it. When that phenomenal expansion of sound has dissolved—meaning it has reached either dissolution or negation—within the Supreme Imperishable which is its own substratum, that which remains as the soundless Brahman is indeed the supreme state (*paramaṃ padam*).

The meaning is "liberation while in the body" (*videhakaivalya*). He praises one who knows this thus: "unstruck" (*anāhata*). It is "unstruck" because it is not produced in the heart, or because it is eternal. The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of proclaiming its eternity.
And so is the statement of the author of the *Bhāṣya-vārttika*: "For the syllable *Oṃ* is eternal," because of the eternity of the *Oṃ*-syllable.

And it is said: "Direct origination is not accepted. Regarding that sound which exists in the form of the *praṇava* consisting of sound, that which is its supreme aspect—the witness-form of both the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and the collective (*samaṣṭi*)—is the supreme, undifferentiated Brahman.
Whatever person, whoever they may be, realizes that [Brahman] as being nothing but their own self (*svamātra*), that yogi has his doubts severed.
He becomes one liberated while in the disembodied state. || 3 ||
The subtlety and all-pervasiveness of Brahman are such that it is a portion of a hundred-thousandth part of the tip of a hair;
half of that portion, and upon the dissolution of even that, is the stainless (nirañjana).
Just as fragrance is within a flower, as ghee is within milk, as oil is within sesame seeds, and as gold is within stones; || 5 ||
Thus, all beings abide in the Self like threads in a gem;
the knower of Brahman, firm in intellect and undeluded, remains established in Brahman.
Just as oil resides within sesame seeds and fragrance is inherent in a flower,
so too does [the Self] abide within the body of a person, both externally and internally.
One should know that the tree is with parts (sakala), while its covering is without parts (niṣkala);
in both the state with parts and the state without parts, the Self is established everywhere.
He describes the supreme subtlety of Brahman—which is accessible only to yogis who have attained such a state—by virtue of its being devoid of distinctions, [saying]:

"The tip of a hair" (*vālāgra*). The tip of a hair, or the awn of a grain of *nīvāra* rice, exists as extremely subtle due to being both visible and invisible; [Brahman is subtler than] a hundred-thousandth part of that.

The consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*) is subtle, being as fine as one-hundred-thousandth part of a *lakṣa*, due to its pervading the subtle individual world (*vyaṣṭiprapañca*); the consciousness of the Lord (*īśvaracaitanya*), which possesses one-hundred-thousandth part of that subtle consciousness residing in the individual soul, is even more subtle.
Because it pervades the collective cosmic egg (*samaṣṭyaṇḍa*), half of that very Lord who possesses such portions— namely,

the fifty-thousandth part consisting of a single portion— is the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), which is most subtle because it pervades its own state of ignorance (*avidyā*) and its effects.

But when the destruction of the qualified [reality] residing in the witnessing consciousness—which depends upon the objects of perception—occurs, then that which is stainless and free from all mental constructs remains as the non-dual Brahman alone, because there is no possibility of anything else existing apart from itself; this is the meaning. (4) But how [is this so]?

To show that the Witness (sākṣin) pervades the state of ignorance, he says: "As flowers," and so forth. Just as fragrance exists pervading flowers, oil exists in sesame seeds, and gold exists in stones; just as thread exists in a collection of jewels, even so the Self of the individual soul (jīvātman) stands within the body of the person, both externally and internally. (5–7)

One should know that the "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) is the entire state of one's own ignorance (*svāvidyāpada*), for it is worthy of being cut down (*vraścana*) or severed by the direct realization of the Lord (*īśvara*). Furthermore, "shadow" (*chāyā*) is Māyā, which covers or veils the tree of the state of ignorance with its own form; it is partless (*niṣkalā*) because it is devoid of constituent parts (*niravayavatvāt*). Thus...

In all states, whether with parts (*sakala*) or without parts (*niṣkala*), in the reality of *māyā*— which, like the shade of a tree, is one's own ignorance (*svāvidyā*) together with its cause— and in all its effects, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is established; He stands pervading it, having permeated all that exists both within and without.

For there is the Vedic revelation: "Nārāyaṇa remains. Alternatively, in the phrase "in the undivided state" (*niṣkale bhāve*), the locative case is used in the sense of the accusative; thus, having previously entered the undivided state during the period of one's own ignorance, that which was everywhere experienced as something other than oneself is, in truth, the Self alone.
The meaning is that it remains established in its own measure alone. || 8 ||
The nature of the Praṇava is the single syllable "Om," which is Brahman; it should be meditated upon as everything by those seeking liberation.
Earth, fire, the Ṛgveda, and the syllable "Bhūḥ" are indeed Pitāmaha (Brahmā).
When dissolution has occurred in the letter 'A', the first part of the Praṇava,
there are the intermediate space, the Yajurveda, Vāyu, the world Bhuvaḥ, Viṣṇu, and Janārdana.
When dissolution has occurred in the letter *u*, the second part of the *praṇava*, then the sky, the sun, and the Sāmaveda are indeed Maheśvara as the vowel *svar*. (11)
When dissolution has occurred in the letter *ma*, which is the third part of the *praṇava*,
the letter *a* becomes yellow in color and is declared to be the quality of *rajas*.
The syllable *ukāra* is sattvic and white; the syllable *makāra* is black and tāmasa.
It has eight limbs, four feet, three locations, and five deities.
He who does not know the syllable *oṃ* cannot be a Brāhmaṇa. To the question of what should be meditated upon by those seeking liberation for that purpose, he says: "Om.
He states its status as the substratum for all negations: "The earth," etc. (9). The word "prāpte" is in the locative case.

The first [syllable] is the primary meaning. By the statement that earth and the other elements attain dissolution into the form of the first part of the *praṇava*, it is indicated that their origination and maintenance also occur therein. Likewise, the intermediate space and so forth, as well as heaven and so forth, undergo origination, maintenance, and dissolution respectively within the syllable *u* and the syllable *m*.
The meaning is that he attains [it]:
Brahmā dissolves into the letter *a*, Hari dissolves into the letter *u*, and Rudra dissolves into the letter *m*; for the Praṇava is remembered as the supreme.

Thus, from such scriptural authority [Śruti] (10–11). It is stated that the vowels *a* and so forth, which are the *mātrās* of the *praṇava*, possess specific colors such as yellow due to their being endowed with the three *guṇas*: "The letter *a*" (12).

He states that the Brahminhood of Brahmins arises from both the knowledge and ignorance of the *praṇava* distinguished by its limbs, feet, stations, and deities— namely, "the eight-limbed" (*aṣṭāṅga*).
The eight limbs consist of the distinctions of *a*, *u*, *m*, the *bindu*, the *nāda*, the *kalā*, that which transcends the *kalā*, and the Supreme (*tatpara*).
That [Self] whose four quarters— by way of the divisions of Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña,

and Turya in the individual (vyaṣṭi), by way of the divisions of Virāṭ, Sūtra, Bīja, and Turya in the collective (samaṣṭi), and by way of the divisions of Ota, Anujñātṛ, Anujñaikarasa, and Avikalpa in the indistinguishable unity of the individual and the collective— are His.
He whose abode or dwelling place consists of the four quarters, the three states beginning with waking, the three bodies beginning with the gross,
the three qualities beginning with sattva, the three powers beginning with the power of action, or the three times beginning with the past— he is the one who has three stations (tristhāna).

He from whose form as a limb the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva attained their divine state—that is the fivefold deity (pañcadaivata). He who knows the Oṃkāra to be such is a Brāhmaṇa, established in Brahman, and liberated while living; he who does not know it thus—[is not so].
The meaning is that he would not be a Brāhmaṇa.
The method for meditating on the Praṇava: the Praṇava is the bow, the Self is indeed the arrow, and Brahman is said to be its target. || 14 ||
One who is vigilant should pierce [the target] like an arrow and become absorbed in that;
when that which is both supreme and inferior is seen, all activities cease.
The gods have their origin in the syllable Oṃ; the vowels have their origin in the syllable Oṃ;
the entire three worlds, including all that is moving and stationary, have their origin in the syllable Oṃ.
The short [Oṃ] burns away sins; the long [Oṃ], imperishable, bestows prosperity;
when joined with the half-mora, the Praṇava grants liberation. || 17 ||
He who knows that which is like an unbroken stream of oil, like the resonance of a long-sounding bell,
the inexpressible tip of the *praṇava*— he is a knower of the Veda.

Since the internal *praṇava* bestows such distinguished fruits, he says "the *praṇava*" to show that for one who knows Brahman through its means, the attainment of its state (*tadbhāvāpatti*) becomes unrestrained.
The internal *praṇava*, consisting of eight *mātrās*, is like a bow.

Because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) serves as the locus for the arrow; for the self (*ātman*) is indeed the arrow, since the mind possesses greater velocity than an arrow. As for what the target is, Brahman is said to be that target, because it is perceived as one's own self. || 14 ||
This very target must be pierced by one who is vigilant and single-minded;

one should maintain the continuous contemplation: "I am indeed Brahman, the inner meaning of the Praṇava. When this is done, just as an arrow becomes submerged in the target, so too one becomes identical with That—Brahman itself.
To the question, "How can there be the attainment of the state of Brahman for that which is active? he says: "They turn back. (15)

Since the vision of Brahman—which is non-different from the supreme, the lower, and the inner self—precedes the renunciation of all activities, [the author] states that the syllable *oṃ*, which has Brahman as its support, is the substratum for all superimpositions: "The syllable *oṃ*," etc. (16).
He states the fruit of the recitation of the *praṇava* according to its short, long, and protracted durations: "If it is short," and so forth.

If it is short, it burns away all evil (*pāpmān*) and one attains immortality (*amṛtatva*). If it is long, one attains great prosperity and attains immortality. If it is protracted (*pluta*), [the same result follows].
"He becomes possessed of knowledge and attains immortality," according to the Śruti. || 17 ||
He states the fruit of the knowledge that transcends the *praṇava* [in the verse beginning] "In oil... (verse 18).
Preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should meditate upon the Praṇava:
one should meditate on the Lord in the form of the syllable Om, the size of a thumb, motionless, resembling a steady lamp-flame in the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus. (19)
Having filled the air through the *iḍā* and having filled it so that it resides within the belly,
one should meditate upon the syllable *Oṃ* situated in the center of the body, surrounded by a mass of flames.
Brahmā is said to be the *pūraka* (inhalation), Viṣṇu is called the *kumbhaka* (retention), and Rudra is proclaimed as the *recaka* (exhalation); these are the deities of *prāṇāyāma*.

To the question "How is the syllable Oṃ to be meditated upon?", he says: "In the heart" (19). To the question "Should it be meditated upon in silence?", he says: "By means of the iḍā. According to the authority of the Śruti, one should join the Praṇava, which has the form of fire, with the fire in the Mūlāgni; thus, [it is to be meditated upon] as blazing intensely within the triangle of the Mūlādhāra.
During the kumbhaka [retention of breath], one should meditate upon the Lord who is the meaning of the syllable Om (praṇava). || 20 ||

He describes the nature of the deities associated with the constituent parts of *prāṇāyāma*: "Brahmā," etc. The meaning is that one should meditate upon Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra during the stages of inhalation (*pūraka*) and so forth. || 21 ||

By another method, one should meditate on the *praṇava*: making the self the lower fire-drill (*araṇi*) and the *praṇava* the upper fire-drill, one shall see [the Self] like a hidden treasure through the practice of churning with meditation. (22)
One should exert one's full strength through the resonance of the sound of the syllable *oṃ*, until the withdrawal of the vital breath, up to the point where the sound completely dissolves.

Those who perceive the single syllable Oṃ— abiding in coming and going yet empty of movement and so forth, radiant as ten million suns, situated within all beings, and consisting of the nature of the Haṃsa— become free from passion.
He describes the meditation on the Lord through another method: "The self," etc.

Having made the self—that is, the internal organ—the lower fire-drill (*adharāraṇi*), and the *praṇava* the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇi*), preceded by the utterance of the *praṇava*, [one should meditate] repeatedly on the meaning of the *praṇava*: "I am Brahman."
Through the continuity of merit and the practice of churning through meditation,
one should thus behold— that is, perceive— the Self as "I am this," like a lamp within a hidden jar. || 22 ||
He states the fruit of the vision of Brahman, which is illuminated at the beginning of the utterance of the *praṇava* and at the end of the resonance (*nāda*) of the *praṇava*:

"The syllable *oṃ*," etc. This refers to that [state] which, by virtue of being the locus for the dissolution of the wind produced by the resonance arising from the utterance of the syllable *oṃ* for as long as one has strength...

That [Self] shines forth through the perspective of one ignorant of oneself as if situated within the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the vital breath (prāṇa), which has the form of sound and the characteristics of coming and going;
yet, through the perspective of one who knows oneself, it is devoid of coming and going, possessing the luster of infinite millions of suns, and is the innermost of all.

The meaning is that those who perceive the Self as the Swan—the form of Brahman non-different from the inner witness—become free from passion (viraja) and have accomplished all that was to be done (kṛtakṛtya). || 23-24 ||
The meditation on Brahman with attributes—that mind which performs the acts of creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the three worlds—dissolves; that is the supreme state of Viṣṇu. (25)
The heart-lotus has eight petals and is endowed with thirty-two filaments;
situated in its center is the sun, and within the sun is the moon.
Fire is situated in the center of the moon; light is situated in the center of the fire;
and the pedestal, encrusted with various jewels, is situated in the center of the light.
In its center was the stainless god Vāsudeva,
whose chest bore the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and who was adorned with pearls and jewels.
One should meditate upon Mahāviṣṇu in this manner, endowed with humility, as resembling pure crystal and possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons. (29)

The mind is the veil of Brahman alone; for one who negates that [mind], Brahman alone shines forth as being without a counterpart. Thus he says: "That which... (verse 25). For one who is unable to meditate in this manner, he describes the method of meditating on Brahman with attributes within the heart-lotus characterized as previously described: [He says: "For one who is unable to meditate thus... etc.

"Eight-petaled" (aṣṭapatram) || 26–28 || This means it is created through such conceptualization (*kalpanā*). If meditation (*dhyāna*) is performed in this way, one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtya*) by means of the knowledge obtained through the purification of the mind gained through its grace.
For one who is too indolent to do so, or for one [practicing] the aforementioned inhalation (*pūraka*) and so forth—
He states the meditation on the triple form (trimūrti): "In this way," etc. (vv. 29–31).

One should meditate upon the threefold form of Mahāviṣṇu, resembling the flax flower, established in the region of the navel; one should contemplate him as four-armed during the pūraka breath-retention.
By means of retention (kumbhaka), one should contemplate the lotus-seated Brahmā, the Grandfather, in the region of the heart— possessing the luster of a precious gem, with four faces.
By means of the *recaka* breath, however, one should [visualize] the Self of Knowledge (vidyātmā), who is three-eyed, situated on the forehead,
resembling pure crystal, partless (*niṣkala*), and the destroyer of sins.
The knower of the Self, who is a meditator distinguished by saguṇa-vidyā, is in reality partless (niṣkala). || 32 ||
In the heart, one should meditate upon that fruit [of yoga]: a lotus with petals below, its flower at the bottom and its stalk above, facing downwards;
resembling a plantain flower, consisting of all the Vedas, and auspicious.
One should visualize there a hundred-petaled lotus with a hundred years of life, its pericarp spread wide;
upon that, one should contemplate the sun, moon, and fire, each positioned above the other.
Having opened the lotus, which possesses the splendor of the sun, moon, and fire, and having extracted its heart-seed syllable, he moves as the Self, firmly established. (35)
He who knows that which has three abodes, three paths, and is the triple Brahman; which consists of three syllables, or three morae, or even half a mora—he is a knower of the Veda.
He who knows that which is like an unbroken stream of oil, like the long resonance of a bell,
the inexpressible tip of the *praṇava*— he is a knower of the Veda.

He describes the heart as the support for meditation in another way: "abja" means that which is born from water, a watery body; "trātaya" means protect it on all sides. Thus, "abjapatra" refers to the lotus of the heart.
It has flowers below because it blooms in its lower part, and it has an upward stalk with its face turned downward.

It resembles the hanging flower of the plantain tree; it consists of all the Vedas because it is the substratum for the sound that is the cause of the Vedas, and for this very reason, it is auspicious (śiva). It lasts for a hundred years because its duration is limited to a lifespan of a hundred years; it is rich in a hundred petals because it is comparable to a lotus with a hundred petals.
Having opened the heart-lotus— which resembles the pericarp of a blooming lotus with its scattered petals—
by means of the *praṇava*, and having turned that heart-lotus upward so that it possesses the radiance of the sun, moon, and fire suspended within, therein...
One should contemplate and meditate upon the mandalas of the sun, moon, and fire, one above the other. Then,
having extracted and grasped the heart-seed syllable called "A" from that heart-lotus, one should conceive of oneself as being fixed in that very form.

Then, there Viṣṇu, whose meaning is the letter *ā*, moves; there is an inversion of the word order—he moves. For one who meditates upon the self as the *haṃsa* in the form of the *praṇava* while it is thus moving, [the scripture] declares the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*) with the words "having three stations" (*tristhāna*).
That which has the three stations beginning with the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep] belongs to him who knows the true nature of reality.
[He is] that which has three paths (trimārga), according to the distinction of the courses of smoke, flame, and so forth, following one's own knowledge;

[he is] that which consists of the three Brahmās (tribrahmātmaka), for whose sake there exists the triad of Brahmās distinguished as Viśva, Virāṭ, and Otrā-Brahman; [he is] that whose limbs are said to be the three syllables beginning with 'A'.

That which has three syllables—meaning that which possesses three measures (*mātrā*) through the division of short, long, and protracted [vowels], or which consists of three measures or even half a measure—he who knows it is a knower of the Veda; the meaning is that he becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). This is in accordance with the Śruti: "The fourth of the fourth, illuminated at the tip of the *oṃkāra*. (36)
He states the fruit of the vision of the tip of the *praṇava* [in the verse beginning] "In oil," etc. (37).
Just as a man might draw up water through the stalk of a lotus, so too should the yogi established on the path of yoga draw the vital breath upward into the abode of Brahman. (38)
Having made the lotus, which serves as a sheath, consist of half a mora,
one should draw it up by means of the stalk alone and lead it to dissolution between the two eyebrows.
One should know that between the eyebrows, on the forehead, and at the root of the nose is the abode of nectar, that great sanctuary of Brahman.

"Having led the outward-moving breath toward the west-facing [aperture], one should dissolve it in the abode of Brahman," so it is said— just as follows: "Just as a man might draw up water through the stalk of a lotus,
even so the yogi, standing on the path of yoga, [draws it] from the *mūlādhāra*."
One should draw upward the vital air (prāṇa) that has attained unity with the downward-moving air (apāna),
leading it upward through the suṣumnā; furthermore,
having attained the state of the gross, subtle, and seed-syllables, it becomes unified with the fires of the gaze.

One should take that lotus of the heart which exists as a treasury, reduce it to its nature of half-a-mātrā, and lead it to dissolution—that is, cause it to attain absorption—in the space between the eyebrows by way of the *suṣumṇā*. || 39 ||
To explain what the locus for the dissolution of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is like, he says:
"But in the middle of the eyebrows" (*bhrūmadhye tu*). This is because the middle of the eyebrows is the place for the realization of Brahman.
By means of the three occurrences of the word "but" (*tu*), [the author implies]: therefore, even though it has gone out from there, one should lead it back again and again to dissolve right there.
It is illuminated. || 40 ||
The six-limbed yoga consists of these six limbs: posture, restraint of the breath, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, and absorption. (41)

Since the dissolution of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the rest into the station of the nectar occurs by way of the *suṣumnā*, and since entry into the *suṣumnā* is not common to all, nor can the path of the *suṣumnā* be touched without the practice of yoga, therefore, the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) serves as the means for that end.
It is said: "The seat. || 41 ||
There are four primary types of seats,
and as many individual seats as there are species of living beings;
Maheśvara alone understands their incomparable varieties.
The fourfold set consisting of Siddha, Bhadra, Siṃha, and Padma—

since there are many varieties of yogic postures (*yogāsana*), he specifies these four beginning with Siddha as being preeminent among them, referring to them as "the postures" (*āsanāni*) because they are beyond numbering.
"Because these are difficult to understand. Regarding the statement that "among those, the four primary postures are established," the scriptural passages that establish them are written here:
"Having pressed the perineum with the left [foot], and the right [foot] above the penis..."
Sitting with the body straight, this shall be the Siddhāsana.
One should place the two ankles below the scrotum on both sides of the perineal seam;
having firmly secured the feet against the sides with the hands so that they are perfectly motionless,
this becomes the Bhadrāsana posture, which destroys poisons and diseases.
Pressing the sīvinī with both ankles in reverse order and extending the hands over the knees, this is the lion-form posture (siṃharūpaka).
When one places both soles of the feet upon the thighs,
this becomes the lotus posture (padmāsana), which removes all diseases and poisons.
Thus [it is said].
The first wheel is the source, the place of origin, and the support; the second is the Svādhiṣṭhāna. || 43 ||
Between those two, the place of origin is called Kāmarūpa.
In the location of the anus, known as the Ādhāra, there is a four-petalled lotus.
In the midst of that, the Yoni named Kāmākhya, adored by the Siddhas, is proclaimed;
likewise, the Liṅga situated within the Yoni faces the west.
He who knows that which is split like a jewel on the head is a knower of Yoga.

Thereafter, he clarifies the nature of the six supports (*ṣaḍādhāra*) and the fruit of knowledge regarding the womb (*yoni*) and so forth of the individual manifestation (*vyāṣṭiprapañca*) situated between the *mūlādhāra* and the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, by means of the verse beginning with "The Support" (*ādhāram*). (43)
It has been stated that the locus of the *yoni* exists between the *mūlādhāra* and the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.

To the question of what kind of *yoni* it is, he says: "The *ādhāra*... (verse 44). In the center of the four petals of the *mūlādhāra*, it is worshipped even by those who have attained success through yoga and those who have not, as it is the cause for the engagement in and withdrawal from the individual cycle of transmigration (*vyaṣṭi-saṃsāra*).

There exists a certain womb called *kāmarūpiṇī*, which is the power *kuṇḍalinī*. Regarding how she is honored by both the perfected (*siddha*) and the unperfected (*asiddha*): if she moves upward from the heart, she becomes the object of worship for the *siddhas* who adorn the path of cessation (*nivṛtti-mārga*). But when, on the other hand—
The meaning is that when it does not move from its own place, it becomes frequented by those in saṃsāra because it is the cause of worldly activity.

Within such a womb, in the central region of Kuṇḍalinī at the level of the head, there is the liṅga of the inner self (pratyagātman), which is like a jewel, distinct, self-luminous, and facing westward.
It exists. Because it reveals both worldly engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), he who knows "I am That" is a knower of Yoga;
the meaning is that he becomes one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), knowing the identity of the inner self and the Supreme. || 45-46 ||
The nature of the four wheels beginning with the Mūlādhāra is like the form of molten gold, flashing like a streak of lightning. (46)
It is quadrangular, situated above the fire and below the penis;
by its own name it is *prāṇa*, and the *svādhiṣṭhāna* is that which rests upon it.
Next, the Svādhiṣṭhāna cakra is said to be the penis itself;
it is like a jewel, wherein the body is filled with wind through the channel.
That navel-center is called the Maṇipūraka-cakra;
in this great twelve-spoked wheel, one is constrained by merit and sin. (49)
The individual soul (jīva) wanders in this manner only so long as it does not find the ultimate reality (tattva).
Thereafter, he describes the nature of the Mūlādhāra: "Taptā... and so forth.
This is because the fire-mandala of the Mūlādhāra-cakra is situated in the middle of the penis (meḍhra). || 46-47 ||

He states the nature of the *svādhiṣṭhāna*: "Sva" [means] the *svādhiṣṭhāna* located at the base of the *liṅga*, endowed with six petals; such is the meaning. He explains the *maṇipūraka*: "Like a jewel" (*maṇivat*) means the *maṇipūraka* is provided with ten petals. After that is the *anāhata-cakra*.

It should be understood that there is a twelve-petaled wheel and a sixteen-petaled wheel of purification (*viśuddhi-cakra*), above which are the lunar and solar mandalas, and above those is a thousand-spoked wheel.
(48–49) Regarding that, he describes the nature of the individual self (*jīvātman*) within the unstruck wheel (*anāhata-cakra*) with the words "twelve," etc. The individual soul situated therein—

As long as one does not know one's own true nature, so long does one transmigrate; the meaning is that when [ignorance] is destroyed by self-knowledge, the individual soul (jīva) is nothing but Brahman. || 49-50 ||
The wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra) is above the penis and below the navel; that which exists there is like the bulbous root (kanda) of a bird’s egg.
Therein, seventy-two thousand channels have arisen;
among those thousands of channels, seventy-two are specifically mentioned. (51)
Among them, ten are remembered as the principal channels that carry the vital breath (prāṇa):
namely, the iḍā, the piṅgalā, and the third, the suṣumnā.
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, and the illustrious Pūṣā; Alambusā and Kuhū are here, and Śaṅkhinī is remembered as the tenth.
Thus, this wheel consisting of the channels (nāḍī) should always be known by yogins;
therein flow perpetually the deities of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, who carry the vital breath (prāṇa). 54.
The three channels known as iḍā, piṅgalā, and suṣumnā have been proclaimed.
The channel iḍā is situated on the left, and piṅgalā is situated on the right. (55)
The Suṣumnā is situated in the middle region; thus, three paths for the vital breath (prāṇa) are traditionally taught.

Thereafter, he describes the location of the root of the channels (nāḍīkanda), its extent, and the nature of the principal channels together with their presiding deities, beginning with the word "above" (ūrdhvam). || 51 ||
53 || For the word *yoginām*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental; thus, it means "by the yogins. Since all of this is clear, it has not been further explained. 54–56 ||
The ten vital airs, beginning with prāṇa, are prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and likewise vyāna; [as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya]. || 56 ||
Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—these five well-known winds beginning with Nāga are known as the Prāṇa and the others. (57)
These, existing in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), reside within the thousands of channels (*nāḍī*).

[The author] now indicates the names of the ten vital winds (*prāṇa*) that move through the channels presided over by the *jīva*: "Prāṇa," etc. (57). Among them, the five beginning with *prāṇa* are renowned as the primary ones, while those beginning with *nāga* are...

The vital airs (vāyu), moreover, are called the secondary breaths (upaprāṇa). Regarding them, he says "these" [in verse 58], explaining that their movement through the channels in the form of the individual soul (jīva) consists of the soul’s incessant coming and going under the influence of the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
The living being is subject to the power of the prāṇa and apāna breaths; for, under the sway of prāṇa and apāna, the living being runs both downward and upward. (58)
Due to its flickering nature, it is not seen by way of the left or right path;
just as a ball, when struck by a staff-like arm, flies upward. (59)
In the same way, the individual soul (jīva), impelled by the prāṇa and apāna breaths, does not rest;
"impelled" is the illustration for its lack of rest. || 59 ||
At the time of yoga, there is a unification of prāṇa and apāna;
the prāṇa draws up from the apāna, and the apāna draws up from the prāṇa.
"He who knows this [method] as being like a rope for birds is a knower of yoga.
Regarding the time of yoga, he states the unification of prāṇa and apāna and the fruit of that knowledge [in the verse beginning] "from apāna":
"From prāṇa, from apāna"—here, the ablative case (pañcamī) has the sense of the accusative (dvitīyārtha). || 60 ||
In the Ajapā Haṃsa-vidyā,
one goes out with the letter *ha* and enters again with the letter *sa*.
The individual soul (jīva) constantly recites this mantra, "haṃsa,
haṃsa," six hundred and twenty-one thousand times day and night.
The individual soul constantly recites this mantra endowed with this number;
it is the Gāyatrī known as Ajapā, which always bestows liberation upon yogins.
By the mere intention of this [mantra], a person is liberated from sins. There is no knowledge equal to this; there is no recitation equal to this. (64)

"A merit equal to this has never existed, nor will it ever exist," he says [in the verse] beginning with "By the syllable *ha*," describing the nature of the recitation (*japa*) of the *haṃsa-vidyā*, which consists of the inhalation and exhalation completed in a single day and night; [this refers to] the activity of the *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and *vyāna* breaths, and the activity of inhalation and exhalation.

This is indeed the *haṃsa-mantra*; that mantra, "haṃsa haṃsa," he describes as having a countable number of repetitions—namely, "hundreds" (verse 62). Even while remaining silent and not reciting it oneself, this [mantra] which attains the state of being recited (*japa*) despite not being recited is called *ajapā*.

The Gāyatrī always bestows liberation upon those yogis who maintain such constant contemplation. Since it is so, [the text says] "of this" (asyāḥ). He praises the Ajapā with the words "by this" (anayā). 64.
By awakening the Kuṇḍalinī, one pierces the door to liberation;
through that path, one must go to the stainless abode of Brahman.
Having covered that opening with her mouth, the Supreme Goddess fell asleep;
she was awakened by the application of fire together with the mind and the vital breath.
Taking hold of the thread like a needle, it ascends through the *suṣumnā*;
just as one might forcibly open a door-panel with a key, so too [should one act]. (67)
In that same way, the yogi should pierce the door of liberation by means of Kuṇḍalinī. || 68 ||
Having joined the palms together, firmly assuming the lotus posture (padmāsana),
placing the chin tightly against the chest, and fixing the mind upon that meditation,
one should repeatedly exhale the apāna wind upward once it has been filled.
Releasing the vital breath, a man attains incomparable awakening through the power of Śakti. || 69 ||

He describes the state of Kuṇḍalinī with the words "by which": according to the Vedic scripture, "The Fourth (turiya) is situated in the head," the Sahasrāra-cakra is the abode of Brahman; for it is there alone that Brahman is perceived by yogins. There, because of the total absence of any impurity distinct from oneself, it is "free from affliction" (nirāmaya). By which... [65]

That [state] is to be reached by way of the *suṣumṇā*; having covered that door with her own mouth, the Supreme Goddess Kuṇḍalinī remains asleep within the belly common to all living beings. As for when she awakens, it is here that the yogi [awakens her] during the state of *kevala-kumbhaka*.
Having been awakened by the fire situated in the *mūlādhāra*, together with the mind and the vital breath (*marut*), [she]—|| 66 ||

Like a fine needle, having taken up the quality of experience (*bhoga*), it proceeds upward through the *suṣumnā* to the *sahasrāra*. He says that one should pierce the mouth of the *suṣumnā* by means of the *kuṇḍalinī*; that is, "one should open it.
Just as a man might forcibly open a door with the effort of a key, so too does the yogi.
The meaning is that one should pierce the excellent Suṣumnā, which is the cause of liberation, by means of Kuṇḍalinī. || 67-68 ||

He states the means for piercing the *suṣumnā* channel, beginning with the word "having": first, the yogi, having assumed the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) and then having joined his hands in the hollowed gesture (*saṃpuṭita*) against his chest,
having placed his chin [upon them] and fixed his meditation upon his own true nature within his mind, repeatedly [drives] the apāna wind upward.
Uttering [the syllable] while contracting [the body], thus releasing the filled vital breath (prāṇa) into the Suṣumnā, the yogi enters the Suṣumnā;

by the power of the Kuṇḍalinī-śakti that has entered the Suṣumnā, he attains the realization of Brahman and the Self, thinking: "I am Brahman, I alone am Brahman"—an incomparable, peerless, and unsurpassed awakening.
Through celibacy and other such practices, the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī occurs;
the yogi seated in the lotus posture, filling the openings of the channels and retaining the vital air within, becomes liberated—of this there is no doubt. (70)
Having massaged his limbs with water produced from physical exertion, he who abandons pungent, sour, and salty foods and delights in drinking milk becomes happy. (71)
A practitioner of yoga who observes celibacy, eats moderately, and is devoted to yoga shall become perfected after one year; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
The power of Kuṇḍalinī is above the *kanda*; that yogi becomes a vessel for the *siddhis*.

Thus he says "in the lotus" (*padme*) to show that one becomes liberated through the *kumbhaka* of the *suṣumnā*. Furthermore, the yogi who, remaining in the *padmāsana*, draws in the external air through the *iḍā*—
Filling the apertures of the channels and retaining the filled air by means of *kumbhaka*, when the yogi causes it to reach the *suṣumnā* and pierces the *brahmarandhra*, that very yogi,
having pierced the *brahmarandhra* and attained that which is to be attained, becomes liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
The meaning is that there is doubt. Regarding this, he states the means: "Of the limbs," etc.

At the beginning, during the stage of practice, perspiration arises at the time of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Having then massaged all the limbs with that [perspiration] and having become firm of body, at that time—

One who renounces pungent, sour, and salty foods, and delights in drinking milk, becomes happy. (71) Having thus become endowed with the observances such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*), one becomes perfected (*siddha*) after a year.
(72) [This applies to] one in whose *suṣumnā* channel, in the upper portion of the *nāḍī*-bulb, resides the power of Kuṇḍalinī.
He would indeed become that very yogi, a recipient of the perfections of yoga.
The three bonds [are attained] through the unification of the apāna and prāṇa breaths and the cessation of urine and feces. || 73 ||
Even an old man becomes young through constant practice of the root-lock (mūlabandha).
One should contract the anus while pressing the perineum with the heel. (74)
Drawing the downward breath upward is called *mūlabandha*. Because of this, the great bird [of the vital breath] performs the *uḍḍīyāna* (the soaring flight) without ceasing. (75)
That indeed is Uḍḍiyāṇa; there the binding is prescribed.
One should perform the backward contraction of the abdomen above the navel. (76)
Furthermore, this Uḍḍiyāṇa-bandha is a lion to the elephant of death;
for it binds the stream of nectar flowing downward from the head. (77)
Then follows the Jālandhara bind, which destroys the flood of suffering in the throat;
when the Jālandhara bind, characterized by the constriction of the throat, has been performed. (78)
As an ancillary to that, he explains the three bonds and their fruit, beginning with "apāna" (verse 73–75).
The contraction of the abdomen is the meaning of "the final protection. || 76 ||

This is the Uḍḍiyāṇa-bandha; it binds—that is, it dries up—the phlegm-water that has arisen in the space of the head and exists in the space of the thousand-petalled lotus (sahasrāra), which takes on the form of all diseases. || 77-78 ||
Through the practice of Khecarīmudrā, the nectar does not fall into the fire, nor does the breath rush away;
the tongue has entered the hollow of the skull and is turned backwards. (79)
The gaze directed between the eyebrows is the Khecarī mudrā;
for one who possesses it, there is neither disease nor death, neither sleep, nor hunger, nor thirst.
And there shall be no fainting for him who knows the Khecarī Mudrā;
he is not afflicted by disease, nor is he tainted by karma.
He for whom the Khecarī-mudrā exists is not bound by time;
because his mind moves in the ether (kha), his tongue becomes one that has gone to the ether. 82.
Therefore, this is the mudrā named Khecarī, which is honored by the Siddhas.

Having explained the three bandhas as limbs of yoga, he now describes the Khecarī mudrā and the fruit resulting from its mastery, beginning with the verse "kapāla... (79). [He also describes] the intermediate fruit of that practice.
But it is not a disease. || 80–82 ||
Through the practice of Khecarī, the perfection of Vajrolī is attained;
by means of the Khecarī mudrā, for whomsoever there is an opening above the uvula.
If the *bindu* of one embraced by a passionate woman leaks away, as long as that *bindu* remains in the body, whence can there be fear of death? (84)
As long as the seal of the sky (nabhomudrā) is bound, the drop (bindu) does not depart;
even when the drop has fallen and reached the circle of the womb (yonimaṇḍala), [it remains]. 85.
One who is bound by the *yonimudrā* ascends forcefully by means of *śakti*.
For one who has mounted the *khecarīmudrā*, there is stability of the *bindu*, which is the cause of life; furthermore, the accomplishment of *vajrolī* occurs.
Thus it is said: "By *khecarī*. By means of the *khecarīmudrā*, the tongue of one [is placed] upon the *lambikā*...
It enters that opening above the uvula. || 83 ||

The word "yat" (which) has the meaning of "tat" (that). The particle "ca" (and) has the sense of "api" (even/also). For him—be he even embraced by a passionate woman—the white drop (*bindu*) does not leak at all. As long as the stability of the drop is achieved, how could the fear of death possibly arise for him? (84) As long as the *khecarī-mudrā*...

The drop (bindu) shall remain bound and not depart as long as it has not fallen; even when the drop has slipped and reached the circle of the womb (yonimaṇḍala), it then ascends upward by force through the power of the Vajroli-refined Yonimudrā.
From the realization of the unity of the two kinds of *bindu*, there is the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatva*).
That very *bindu* is of two kinds: white and likewise red. (86)
They say that which is pale is white, while that called red is the great dye;
the menstrual flow (rajas), resembling coral trees, resides in the place of the womb.
The *bindu* resides in the place of the moon; the unification of these two is very difficult to attain.
The *bindu* is Śiva, and the *rajas* is Śakti; the *bindu* is the moon, and the *rajas* is the sun. (88)
Only from the union of both is the supreme form attained, just as dust in the sky is driven by the wind that moves the power (śakti). 89.
When it attains oneness with the Sun, it then becomes a divine body;
the white [element] joined with the Moon, and the Rajas joined with the Sun. (90)
He who knows the state of equanimity between the two is a knower of Yoga.
He says that through the awakening to their unity, one attains the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), based on the twofold nature of the *bindu*—that very [state] being such.
(86) The place of the womb (*yonisthāna*) is situated in the *mūlādhāra*; therein resides *rajas*, the principle of the Goddess (*devītattva*).
Or it is called the *jīva* (the individual soul). [Verse 87] The space between the eyebrows and the center of the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*) is the abode of the moon;
there dwells the *bindu*, the *śivatattva*. The unity of these two—Śiva and Śakti, or the *jīva* and the Supreme (*para*)—is difficult for anyone to attain except for a yogin. [Verses 88–90]

The meaning is that he who knows the union of the moon and the sun situated within the thousand-spoked [lotus] between the eyebrows— which consists of the forms of white and red— becomes a knower of yoga and a knower of Brahman.
The practice of Mahāmudrā is the purification of the web of impurities and the union of the moon and the sun. || 91 ||
The thorough drying up of the fluids is correctly termed Mahāmudrā. || 92 ||
Placing the shins upon the chest and pressing the vaginal opening with the left foot,
while supporting the extended right foot with both hands,
one fills the two sides of the abdomen with breath and slowly exhales.
Indeed, this Mahāmudrā is proclaimed as the destroyer of the sins of men. || 93 ||

The characteristic of Mahāmudrā is described as "purification. This refers to the purification of the mass of impurities residing in the channels by means of the water of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*)—consisting of exhalation, inhalation, and retention—which is accomplished through various yogic methods; it is the unification of the moon and the sun, and the [balancing] of the humors such as wind and bile.
And that by which drying occurs is designated as "Mahāmudrā. || 91-92 ||
Regarding the practice of Mahāmudrā, it says "the chest" (*vakṣa*): first, the yogin, having applied the Jālandhara-bandha and pressing the vaginal cavity with his left foot,
while holding his extended right leg with both hands, fills the pair of bellies with breath and then performs the retention (*kumbhaka*).

One should exhale slowly through the *iḍā* [left nostril]. This method, which destroys all sins for men and removes obstacles to yoga for practitioners, is called the *mahāmudrā*. Thus, *prāṇāyāma* has been described.
*Pratyāhāra* is the withdrawal of the sense of "I" (egoity) residing in the non-self, such as the body and so forth, back toward the inner self (*pratyak*).
The firm conviction that Brahman is indeed the inner self is *dhāraṇā*. The steady contemplation, "I am Brahman; I am indeed Brahman," is *dhyāna*.

The dissolution of the conceptualization of the triad beginning with meditation (dhyāna) is non-conceptual samādhi; since it has been asserted that "yoga is said to have six limbs," the meaning is that, in accordance with that [assertion], one should infer the presence of withdrawal (pratyāhāra) and the other limbs even though they are not explicitly mentioned in the response. || 93 ||
The direct realization of the Self within the heart:

Now I shall explain the determination of the Self. In the location of the heart, there exists an eight-petalled lotus; in its center, having drawn a circular line, [one perceives] the form of the individual soul (*jīvātman*), which is of the nature of light and the size of an atom.
It proceeds. In that [state], everything becomes established; it knows everything, it does everything, and it conducts itself in this manner:

"I am the doer, I am the speaker, I am happy, I am miserable, I am one-eyed, I am lame, I am deaf, I am mute, I am thin, I am fat"—thus it proceeds according to the doctrine of independence. || 93-94 ||

When it rests on the eastern petal—the eastern petal being white in color—then the mind becomes inclined toward dharma preceded by devotion. (93-2) When it rests on the southeastern petal—the southeastern petal being red in color—then the mind becomes inclined toward sleep and laziness. (93-3) When [it rests] on the southern petal...

When it rests upon that southern petal, which is black in color, then the mind becomes characterized by hatred and anger. || 93-4 || When it rests upon the southwestern petal, that southwestern petal being blue in color, then the mind becomes intent on evil deeds and violence. || 93-5 || When it rests upon the western petal...
Then, the western petal is crystal-colored, and at that time, the mind becomes intent on playful diversion. || 93-6 ||
When it rests upon the petal of the northwest, the northwest petal being the color of ruby,
then the mind becomes inclined toward travel, movement, and renunciation. When it rests upon the northern petal,
that northern petal being yellow in color, then the mind becomes inclined toward pleasure and amorous passion.
When it rests upon the northeastern petal, that northeastern petal is the color of lapis lazuli;

at that time, there arises a mind of compassion for giving and other virtues. When the mind resides in the joints between the petals, then there occurs the provocation of the great diseases of wind, bile, and phlegm.

When it stands in the center, then one knows everything, sings, dances, recites, and experiences bliss. (93–11) When there is eye fatigue, for the sake of removing that fatigue, one forms a circle of the first line and performs immersion in the center; this is the first line.

Then, having the color of the bandhūka flower, there occurs the state of sleep (*nidrāvasthā*). Within the state of sleep, there occurs the state of dreaming (*svapnāvasthā*). Within the state of dreaming, one constructs conceptualizations (*kalpanā*) such as what has been seen, heard, inferred, or reported; that is the beginning of fatigue.

[It] occurs. || 93-12 || For the purpose of removing fatigue, one forms a second line as a circle and causes it to submerge into the center; when the second line is the color of Indra’s wrath (Indrakopa), then the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) occurs.
In deep sleep, the intellect (*buddhi*) becomes related solely to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).
Thereafter, she becomes of the nature of eternal consciousness, and attainment occurs in the form of the Supreme Lord.
Having formed a circle with the third line, it causes immersion in the center; when the third line is the color of a ruby, then the fourth state (turīya) arises in the fourth.

When the mind becomes related solely to the Supreme Self and one becomes of the nature of eternal consciousness, then, by means of the intellect held with fortitude, one should gradually come to rest;
having fixed the mind in the Self, one should not think of anything at all. (93–14)

Then, having unified the prāṇa and apāna, one holds the entire universe as the object of focus within the nature of the Self; when that is the state beyond the fourth (turīyātīta), then one becomes the very nature of bliss for all and transcends dualities, remaining as long as the maintenance of the body persists.
Thereafter, attainment occurs in the form of the Supreme Self; in this manner liberation comes about, and this alone is the means for the realization of the Self. || 93-15 ||
When the breath, joined with the path of the senses and the great door, moves upward through the triangle situated within it, the Imperishable One is perceived. 94.

Anticipating the doubt as to how the determination of the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) might be achieved, the most compassionate Śruti explains the determination of the Supreme Self along with its means, beginning with the word "Now" (*atha*). Now, following the attainment of the aforementioned qualification,
the Śruti intends to explain the true nature of the Self together with its means.

Thus he said: "In the heart. Having drawn a circular line within the center of the eight-petaled heart-lotus and visualized it as being round in shape, one perceives that in its center there exists the support of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is in the form of the light of the *haṃsa*, the nature of the individual soul (*jīvātman*), and is of the size of an atom. In that which thus exists, everything resides.

It is established [in him] because he is the locus of everything; for he knows everything and performs everything—meaning that while acting with the conceit "I am the doer," he exists as one for whom everything that ought to be done is already accomplished. (93-1) Regarding his possession of the functions of *dharma* and so forth due to the connection with the petals of the east and other directions, [the author] says:
Regarding the word "pūrva" (eastern): this very one called the individual soul (*jīva*), the *ahaṃ-haṃsa*, when [it is] upon the eastern petal... [93-2-93-13]
Therefore, having thus bypassed everything from the eastern petal up to the second line and relying instead upon the third line,

one realizes Brahman as the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta)— the very nature of the fourth (turya), established through the negation of all portions to be discarded, beginning with the fourth and ending with the cosmic (viśva).

"It remains as that alone, which is its own nature free from all correlates"—thus he says: "Then, gradually... (93-14). If there arises the emergence of any activity distinct from itself, then [one attains] the unification of the prāṇa and apāna, and so forth. The entire universe is to be perceived as the very nature of the Self.

It maintains [the state], because the Brahman—which is established as free from all that is to be abandoned—is characterized by its own remaining essence. When such a state is thus characterized, then this is that fourth state (*turīyāvasthā*).
As long as there is the maintenance of the body, it remains an attainment, even if it exists merely as a phenomenal appearance.
The meaning is this: first, one relies on the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) through the realization "I am the body";
subsequently, following the awakening that "nothing exists apart from oneself," one becomes the Supreme Self alone. In this manner, liberation occurs even while living.
The meaning is that this alone is the means for the vision of the Self, and nothing else. || 93-15 ||
He states the means for those of dull intellect to perceive the Self: "At the crossroads" and so forth.
The "crossroads" is the *jālandhara-bandha*; that which goes to the "great gate," the aperture of the *suṣumnā*, conjoined with that [bandha], is the "great-gate-goer," and that is the wind (*vāyu*).
The Great Gate-Cow Wind; together with that Great Gate-Cow Wind, [the breath] moves from the root of the triangle at the base (mūlādhāra) upward into the suṣumnā situated at the mūlādhāra.

The meaning is that by the mere entry of the sight, the vital breath, the fire, and the mind into Kuṇḍalinī, the Supreme Self—which has not fallen away from its own measure—is seen; that is to say, it is directly realized. || 94 ||
Through the continuous contemplation of the *nāda*, the vision of the Self arises.
Above the previously mentioned location of the triangle, one should meditate upon the five-colored elements beginning with earth.
Furthermore, there are the five vital airs beginning with *prāṇa*, as well as their seed-syllables (*bīja*), phonemes (*varṇa*), and locations (*sthāna*).
The syllable *ya* is the seed-syllable of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), resembling a dark blue cloud;
and the syllable *ra* is the seed-syllable of fire (*agni*), resembling the sun of the downward breath (*apāna*). || 95 ||
The letter *la* is the form of the earth, the pervasive breath (*vyāna*), resembling the bandhūka flower;
the letter *va* is the seed-syllable of the individual soul (*jīva*), the upward-moving breath (*udāna*), with the color of a conch shell.
The letter *ha* has the nature of space (*viyat*), is equal [to it], and possesses the luster of crystal;
it is situated in the heart, the navel, the nose, the throat, the big toes, and other parts of the body. (97)
It moves within seventy-two thousand channels;
it is established in twenty-eight million pores of the skin. (98)

The vital breath is common [to all], yet the individual soul (jīva) is indeed one and the same; with a steady mind and concentrated focus, one should perform the three-fold practice beginning with exhalation (recaka). 99.
Having slowly drawn everything inward into the hollow of the heart-lotus and having bound the prāṇa and apāna breaths, one should utter [the mantra] with the praṇava.
Having performed the contraction of the throat as well as the contraction of the *liṅga*, [one perceives] the *suṣumnā* from the *mūlādhāra*, auspicious and resembling a lotus fiber. 101.
The sound arising from the neck of a lute exists as formless, just like the resonance in the middle [of the body] produced by the sound of a conch shell and other such instruments. || 102 ||
The sound that has entered the aperture of space is indeed the peacock-like sound (māyūra-nāda),
located in the middle of the hollow of the skull, at the center of the four gates.
Then that Self shines there like the sun in the sky;
indeed, between the two bows, within the apertures of Brahmā, is the Śakti.
One should perceive one's own self as the Puruṣa, with the mind having attained dissolution therein;
[one perceives] the jewels, the sound of moonlight, the Bindu, and the station of Maheśvara.
The person who knows this attains absolute liberation.
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.

Thus, demonstrating the attainment of that state for those who have not yet achieved direct realization through the means of following the resonance (*nāda*), he concludes with the verse beginning "pūrva" [etc.]. What is the object of meditation? It is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth.
If this is so, then by that [means], one whose mind is unripe...
Above the previously mentioned fire-mandala of the trikona at the mūlādhāra, one should meditate upon that which is born from the vital airs such as prāṇa,
endowed with the five colors beginning with earth. One should meditate upon the seed-syllable beginning with the letter *ya*,
colored like a dark blue cloud, and distinguished by its location in the heart and other centers.
The connection is with what precedes. First, one should know the letter *ya* in the heart as the seed-syllable of *prāṇa*;

it should be understood that one should know *prāṇa* as being distinguished by a color equal to a dark blue cloud. One should know the letter *ra* in the anus as the seed-syllable of fire (*agni*) and *apāna*, resembling the sun. [It is] the seed-syllable of earth.
One should know the syllable *la* to be like the bandhūka flower, representing the *vyāna* breath that pervades the entire body.
One should know the syllable *va* in the region of the throat to be the seed-syllable of the individual soul (*jīva*), representing the *udāna* breath and distinguished by the color of a conch shell.

One should know that the letter *ha* is the seed-syllable of space (*viyat*), which is equal to the *samāna* breath and has the luster of crystal. In this way, one should know that the five vital breaths (*prāṇapañcaka*) are situated in the heart, the navel, the nose, the throat, the big toes of the feet, and so forth.
97. Therein, the *samāna* wind, constantly moving through the seventy-two thousand channels of the body, remains pervading the twenty-eight million pores of the skin. 98.

When investigated, however—the word "however" (*tu*) serves for emphasis—the various winds beginning with *samāna* and ending with *prāṇa* are indeed one. That which is the support of these five vital breaths is this very *jīva*, who is one alone. The word "indeed" (*hi*) indicates well-known fact. Having understood it thus, then...

"Next, the exhalation and so forth. Thus, having understood the nature of the individual soul (jīva) as mounted upon the five vital breaths (prāṇas) as previously described, the yogi, with a firm mind and becoming concentrated, should perform the three types of breath control (prāṇāyāma), each characterized by the three stages beginning with exhalation (recaka). Slowly.
Having drawn in the thousandfold fluctuations of one's own internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) into the hollow of the heart-lotus,
and having bound both the prāṇa and apāna breaths right there,
one should repeatedly utter the thousand-spoked wheel of the Command (ājñā-sahasrāra-cakra) by means of the *praṇava* alone— that is, the *praṇava* itself— and lead it upward. 100.

As a means to that end, the mention of "constricting and grasping the throat-ligament" (kaṇṭhaliṅga-saṃkocana-grahaṇa) is intended as an indication of the three bindings (bandha-traya). Thus, having performed the three bindings, starting from the Mūlādhāra—that is, beginning from the Mūlādhāra—the auspicious Suṣumnā, which resembles a lotus fiber, [is to be raised]; and by the word "and" (ca), [the other two channels are also included].

It is indicated that within that [space], the channel of absolute liberation (*kaivalyanāḍī*) is established. Therein, the formless sound (*nāda*) exists, having arisen from the neck of the lute which is the support of the *suṣumnā*. For this very reason, the middle of the lute-neck itself is the place of origin of the sound, just as [in the case of a lute].
And by means of the sound of a conch-shell and so forth, the resonance (nāda) that has entered the aperture of the heart-sky becomes manifest.
When this resonance imitates the very resonance of a peacock,
then, through the division of the four doors— namely Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumnā, and Ghaṇṭikā— it resides in the center.
Within the hollow of the skull (kapāla), when the sun is in that space, so too does the Supreme Self shine forth, becoming perfectly manifest; there, where the mind— characterized by sight,
wind, fire, kuṇḍalinī, and so forth— has reached dissolution.

In the apertures beginning with the *mūlādhāra* up to the realization of Brahman, and between the two bows—the word "tu" (but/indeed) having the sense of "yathā" (as)—one should behold one's own self as the Puruṣa, according to one's capacity and according to one's strength. What is it qualified by? Here [it is said]: "arisen from the thunderbolt-staff."

And according to the scriptural statement "there are twenty-one jewels," there are twenty-one jewels of the Fourth (turīya), beginning with "Viśva-turīya" and ending with "Avikalpānujñaikarasa"; their "Jyotsnī" is the luminous substratum.
It does not grant the fourteen-fold conceptualizations beginning with waking-within-waking; thus it is *nada*.
That very thing is *nāda*, the fourth-of-the-fourth (*turya-turya*), the point (*bindu*) whose nature is devoid of distinction.
And because He is the Great Lord (*maheśvara*)—the Sovereign capable of abiding as the mere Great Brahman (*brahma-mātra*) which is free from all correlates—He is Maheśvara.

The state of being that is *māheśvara* (belonging to Maheśvara); the connection with the preceding [verse] is: "the wise man should see the *pada* as 'it abides' (*padate*) by virtue of its own nature alone. (105) He concludes while stating the fruit of knowledge:
"He who... Here, the meaning is that at the very moment of realization, the wise man remains in the form of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).

"Upon knowing Brahman, one becomes Brahman itself"— since this scriptural statement declares that the attainment of the state of being Brahman alone occurs at the very same moment as knowledge, this word "Upanishad" marks the conclusion of the Dhyānabindu Upanishad. || 106 ||
This concise and clear commentary on the Dhyānabindu has been written by Upaniṣadbrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra.
The Dhyānabinduvivaraṇa consists of three hundred and thirty [verses].
[Thus ends the commentary on the Dhyānabindu Upaniṣad, completing the thirty-ninth number in the exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Śrīmad Īśa.]
